# Misfire! Does Good Compression Mean There Are No Valve Issues?

A persistent misfire on a single cylinder that refuses to yield to standard ignition swaps is frustrating, but the diagnostic path you've taken so far actually points in the right direction. You have an O-series engine from 1991 with Cylinder 1 misfiring under load, yet swapping plug leads, caps, and plugs yields no change. The spark is strong and consistent, timing is verified, andâcruciallyâstatic compression on that cylinder reads 150 psi, matching the other cylinders perfectly.

It is entirely logical to conclude that high static compression rules out significant valve leakage. If the intake or exhaust valves were leaking enough to cause a misfire, you would expect a measurable drop in compression pressure. However, the nuance lies in the difference between what a compression test measures and what the engine actually needs to run smoothly.

A standard compression test is a snapshot of volume displacement at a single point in the cycle. It confirms that the cylinder can hold air when the piston is at Top Dead Center (TDC) on the compression stroke. It does not, however, guarantee that the valves are sealing perfectly under the dynamic conditions of combustion or that they are timing their opening and closing events with absolute precision during operation.

Consider the scenario where an intake valve is slightly bent but still closes enough to pass a 150 psi test. During the power stroke, the pressure builds rapidly. If the valve face is warped by even a fraction of a millimeter, that seal might hold during compression but fail under the higher pressures and temperatures of combustion, allowing hot gases to escape into the intake tract. This loss of peak cylinder pressure reduces torque output without necessarily dropping the static compression reading below normal thresholds.

Furthermore, your observation about the engine running "just fine" on three cylinders when warm is a significant data point. The fact that it labors uphill and suffers poor fuel economy in this configuration suggests a severe power deficit, yet the engine continues to run. This behavior often indicates an issue with ignition synchronization or mechanical interference rather than a complete valve failure. If the misfire were purely due to a leaking exhaust valve, you would likely hear distinct popping sounds from the exhaust pipe when the van is under load, as unburnt fuel ignites in the downstream system.

The fact that detaching the spark plug lead makes virtually no difference implies that the ignition coil and distributor are functioning correctly for that cylinder. The engine is essentially running on three cylinders with one doing nothing but spinning. This points toward a potential issue with the mechanical valve timing or a very specific condition of the intake/exhaust valves that isn't caught by a static test.

If you suspect valve issues despite good compression, do not rely solely on feeling for lift or listening for ticking while the engine is cold, as these methods are unreliable. The most definitive way to verify valve integrity in this context is a wet compression test. Adding oil to the spark plug hole and retesting can reveal ring issues, but more importantly, if you suspect valve seating problems, a leak-down test is superior. A leak-down test pressurizes the cylinder while the piston is at TDC and listens for escaping air. If you hear air hissing into the intake or exhaust, you have confirmed a valve seal issue regardless of the static compression number.

In your specific case, since the engine runs better warm, thermal expansion might be temporarily sealing minor gaps that exist when cold. However, relying on this behavior is risky. The high load demand of climbing hills requires maximum cylinder pressure; any latent leakage becomes critical under these conditions. Before condemning the valve covers or timing chain, a leak-down test will provide the definitive answer: does the air escape through the valves (indicating a need for valve adjustment or replacement) or through the crankcase breather (indicating piston ring issues)?

If the leak-down test confirms that air is escaping past the valves despite the 150 psi compression, the solution is likely a valve job or replacing the timing chain if there has been any slack. Static compression tests are useful for ruling out catastrophic failures like blown head gaskets or broken pistons, but they are not a substitute for a leak-down test when diagnosing subtle valvetrain issues.
